extracted.subtask_description: Official examination guidance for assessing patentability and specification/claim drafting issues across textile, architectural-design, and computer-related inventions. Covers claim construction, enablement, novelty/inventive-step assessment, subject-matter eligibility, and examination searching scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fiber invention specified with manufacturing method
rubrics_metrics.description: When an invention is specified by a spinning/manufacturing method, novelty and inventive step may be shown by examples and comparative examples considering technical characteristics that give suitable properties to the undrawn fiber formed immediately after spinning by heat treatment and drawing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not construe a claim relating to fiber material specified with a spinning method to be limited by an embodiment in the description; instead construe it to include the whole span of fiber material properties possible to produce according to the specified method. Use comparative examples to prove difference from prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Textile invention with additional design feature
rubrics_metrics.description: Textile inventions whose main characteristic is exterior beauty (design) are evaluated subjectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the design effect is generated merely by a textile structure or process method that is obvious to a person skilled in the art or each feature is disclosed in prior art, the invention lacks inventive step. However, if the structure of the design has a new technical function, patentability can be recognized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determination of effect revealed by limited shape
rubrics_metrics.description: Minute differences in shape of components (e.g., ring, traveler, metallic card clothing, knitting needle) may greatly influence the result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the effect arising from any shape difference; when there is doubt about the effect because it is difficult to be sure, consider test data or certified test results to establish the technical effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examination of textile inventions related to traditional art
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications involving traditional art (knowledge passed from masters to pupils) may be difficult to examine by patent-document search alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search non-patent documents (e.g., documentation of traditional methods). For traditional-art improvements (e.g., natural dyeing), compare technical characteristics of the improved method with prior art in the field to determine inventive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of related technical fields for textile machinery inventive-step search
rubrics_metrics.description: Textile industry inventions (especially machinery) may relate to general machine engineering and other technical fields beyond textile IPC classes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expand prior-art search beyond related IPC (D section) to general machinery and other technical fields (e.g., general chemistry for PTFE/polyimide compounds). Consider non-patent documents (device guidelines, catalogs) that may not be in the Patent Search System and assess levels of well-known prior art in other fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification requirements for architectural-design inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Architectural-design inventions combine space(s) with function(s); functions of spaces must be stated in claim(s) and the description, and interactions among unit-space functions should be described when the functional effect is not recognizable from placement alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When shape and structure of things are directly stated in claims, also state the function of the space and interactions among functions in the specification to adequately define the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of invention category for architectural-design claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Because architectural-design expressions (apartment design, floor plan, structure system, plan system) may blur whether the claim is for a product or a method, the category of claimed subject matter must be clear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clearly specify whether the invention is a product (e.g., apartment), a method for constructing a product, or a method for designing. Example: a claim described as a 'method of designing' but actually claiming a product combination should be recast as a product claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure timing / public distribution of design documents
rubrics_metrics.description: Design documents (drawings, specifications, structure calculation sheets, HVAC calculation sheets) are prepared for construction and may be distributed; whether submission to public office constitutes public disclosure depends on access.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize distribution time when a person not under confidentiality can access the specification. Submission to a public office for construction permission does not automatically equal public disclosure; however, documents published in public gazettes (e.g., city plan) are considered distributed and public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject-matter eligibility for architectural-design inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: An architectural-design invention is an invention on a construction (product) or a method relating to a construction; it must achieve purpose/effect via functions of unit spaces and interactions among those functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims must specify functions of unit spaces or products forming unit spaces and, if necessary, interactions among functions to complete the invention. Function alone is not the invention; claim a product embodying the function(s) and interactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty and inventive-step assessment for architectural-design inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Objectives and effects of architectural-design inventions are associated with function of unit spaces and interactions among functions; when assessing novelty/inventive step, function and effect must be considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not construe claims by excluding the function; excluding function may make the claim too broad and render it non-novel in view of prior art with identical components but different objectives/effects (example: housing unit vs hospital). Consider function and effect based on differences in space functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categories for computer-related invention claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Computer-related inventions may be claimed as (1) method inventions (series of steps), (2) product inventions (specify multiple functions performed), (3) computer-readable-medium claims with program code recorded to install/execute/distribute, and (4) computer-readable-medium claims with data recorded when the data structure determines operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that recite 'computer program recorded in a medium' (or compatible terms) are allowed; claims to a computer program per se (not recorded in a medium) are not allowed. Example claim formats are provided for each category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indefiniteness from ambiguous actor in 'using a computer' claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims phrased as 'using a computer, comprising the steps of ...' can be indefinite regarding who (human or computer) performs each step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claim can be construed both as a human operating a computer as a mere tool and as an information-processing method by computer software, it is indefinite. Draft claims to clarify whether steps are performed by human operators or by computer-implemented means.

rubrics_metrics.name: Program-as-means definiteness requirement for medium claims
rubrics_metrics.description: A program recorded on a medium makes the computer operate as functional means, but the program per se does not function as a 'means'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To be definite, phrase claims to reflect that the program makes the computer operate as specific functional means (e.g., 'the program makes the computer operate as an order-receiving means...') rather than implying the program itself is a functional means.

rubrics_metrics.name: Undefined-terms lead to indefiniteness
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim uses uncommon technical terms, abbreviations, or symbols that are not defined in the specification and are not common general knowledge, the claimed invention is unclear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure terms used in claims are defined in the description or are part of common general knowledge at the filing date; otherwise provide definitions to avoid indefiniteness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to specify technical relationships among elements
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is unclear when it fails to specify the technical relationships between elements that define the invention (e.g., mere statement that a program is being transmitted does not define a product invention).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims must specify technical relationships (how elements interact or are structured) so that the invention can be recognized as a technical product or process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Category clarity for program signals/products/outputs
rubrics_metrics.description: Ambiguity about which category subjects like program signals, program signal sequences, program products, and program outputs fall into makes claims unclear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify the category (product, method, medium) for such subject matter in claims and descriptions so examiners can properly assess them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid vague qualitative expressions (e.g., 'high speed') in claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Using comparative or qualitative adjectives without objective criteria (e.g., 'high speed') obscures claim scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Either remove such vague terms or provide objective criteria (thresholds, measurements) to make the scope clear; otherwise recast claim to avoid the vague qualifier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims reciting only results without means are indefinite
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that recite solely the results to be accomplished (functions) without specifying concrete means, products, or processes are not recognizably claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the following determinative points for function-defined claims: (i) if a person skilled in the art can introduce specific matter(s) realizing the function from the claim plus common general knowledge, the claim scope is clear; (ii) if not, scope is generally unclear; (iii) exceptions exist where the specification/drawings properly define the matter only with function; (iv) if the connection between function and technology level is hard to understand, the scope can be considered unclear because novelty/inventive-step/violation assessments are impractical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement requirement for computer-related inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: The description must enable a person skilled in the art, using ordinary technical means and ordinary creative activity, to carry out the claimed invention on the basis of the specification, drawings, and common general knowledge as of the filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the description provides sufficient detail for implementation; if not, notify rejection under Patent Act 42(3)(i).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of enablement violations (computer-related)
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical enablement violations include: (1) use of uncommon terms/abbreviations/symbols without definition; (2) abstract statements of steps/functions without disclosure of implementation on hardware/software; (3) GUI-only explanations without implementation details; (4) functional block diagrams/flowcharts insufficient to show hardware/software structure; (5) mismatch between function-defined claims and flowchart-only embodiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When these issues are found, determine that the invention cannot be carried out by a skilled person and issue the appropriate exam findings. Provide concrete implementation details or program listings with sufficient explanation where needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notes on description sufficiency and program listings
rubrics_metrics.description: When descriptions use functional or operational terms, particular attention must be paid to clarity and completeness for enablement; short program listings in common languages may be included with explanations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a skilled person would not be able to carry out the invention, notify rejection under Patent Act 42(3)(i). A program listing may be submitted as a reference with sufficient explanation, but the specification cannot be amended based solely on that reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability subject-matter criteria for computer-related inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: To be statutory subject matter, a computer-related invention must be 'a creation of technical ideas utilizing a law of nature.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If information processing by software is concretely implemented using hardware resources such that a particular machine or operational method particularly suitable for a use purpose is constructed by concrete means with cooperative software and hardware working to perform arithmetic operations or information manipulation, the invention (software/apparatus/method/medium) may qualify as technical subject matter. Business-related inventions generally require specific hardware implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure to assess subject-matter eligibility (computer-related)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment proceeds by: (1) understanding the claimed invention from the claim language; (2) determining whether information processing by software is concretely implemented by using hardware resources; (3) if not concretely implemented, concluding the claimed invention does not constitute a creation of technical ideas utilizing a law of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this three-step check. Example: a computer that contains input/processing/output means that 'prepares a summary' does not necessarily show cooperative concrete implementation; if the processing means cannot be said to cooperatively work to concretely implement the information processing, the claim may not be statutory.
